id: #104 from The Poems of Gaius Valerius Catullus

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

with Dana Ward with Dana Ward I have so little want of activity even writing with its pain more terrible than life I don’t want but do because I’m kind of stupid finally not in the way, you, Sarah know I am nor, you reader, who think of me fishing. Line, spindle, lure, bait. Instruments for me are accessories, even the matchbook is only a tiara to my eyes, the fishing lure a long & white bracelet. Some of my so-called friends think of me as a derelict they always try to hold me to account. “Tell me what happened on the drunken night in question” On the witness stand I am a kitten terribly cute but I can’t say a thing about stupid, or fish, or last night. I like to lay at the base of a hill asleep while the shepherds work bringing things to heel with tepid will where I source my contempt in the index of swill. The entries there make no mention of hell which was sifted through the vale of tears, & fell to make Earth, & the base of this hill where I sunbathe & murmur ‘jealous cellmate’ as my willful peers go by.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker expresses a profound lack of desire for activity, including writing, yet continues to write despite its pain.
- Fishing tools and other instruments are viewed not for their practical uses but as decorative accessories.

prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The speaker explores apathy, the pain of writing, social judgment, and unreliable memory through surreal images of fishing gear, a witness stand, and pastoral idleness. These images portray withdrawal and contempt as defenses against demands for accountability, revealing a self trapped between willful peers and a desire to remain passive and unknowable.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Dana, Ward, Sarah

outputs.L1:
With Dana Ward, with Dana Ward, I have so little desire for activity. Even writing, with its pain more terrible than life, I don’t want—but do—because I’m kind of stupid. Finally, not in the way you, Sarah, know I am, nor you, reader, who think of me fishing: line, spindle, lure, bait.

Instruments, for me, are accessories. Even the matchbook is only a tiara to my eyes; the fishing lure, a long white bracelet. Some of my so-called friends think of me as a derelict. They always try to hold me to account: “Tell me what happened on the drunken night in question.”

On the witness stand, I am a kitten—terribly cute—but I can’t say a thing about stupid, or fish, or last night. I like to lie asleep at the base of a hill while the shepherds work, bringing things to heel with tepid will, where I source my contempt in the index of swill.

The entries there make no mention of hell, which was sifted through the vale of tears and fell to make Earth—and the base of this hill, where I sunbathe and murmur, “jealous cellmate,” as my willful peers go by.
outputs.L2:
Beside Dana Ward—beside Dana Ward—I feel almost no urge to act. I do not even wish to write, an agony more dreadful than living, yet I write anyway, perhaps because I am somewhat foolish. At last, though, not foolish in the manner you, Sarah, recognize, nor in the manner imagined by you, reader, picturing me angling: cord, reel, hook, bait. To me, tools are merely adornments. A matchbook becomes a crown before my eyes; a pale, elongated lure becomes a bracelet.

Certain people who call themselves my friends regard me as a wreck and repeatedly demand an explanation: “Describe what occurred during the drunken evening under discussion.” Put me on the witness stand and I turn into an unbearably adorable kitten, unable to utter anything about idiocy, fish, or the previous night.

I prefer sleeping at the foot of a hill while shepherds labor, weakly forcing everything into order. There, in the catalog of slop, I obtain my scorn. Its records say nothing of hell: hell was strained through the valley of sorrow, then dropped down to form the Earth, this hillside’s foundation, and the very spot where I bask in sunlight, whispering “envious prison companion” as my deliberately determined equals pass me.
outputs.L3:
The speaker expresses a profound aversion to activity, including writing itself. Although the act of writing causes pain, the speaker continues, revealing a tension between creative compulsion and a desire to withdraw from all effort. This detachment also shapes the speaker’s perception of practical objects: fishing tools and other instruments are valued less for their intended functions than for their appearance as decorative accessories.

The speaker’s friends interpret this attitude as irresponsible. They demand explanations for episodes of drunken behavior, but the speaker insists that no coherent account can be given. Rather than joining others in their efforts to work, organize, and impose order, the speaker would prefer to sleep and sunbathe at the foot of a hill.

Throughout the passage, this rejection of responsibility is accompanied by sharp contempt for willful, judgmental peers. Surreal images of hell, Earth, and a “jealous cellmate” transform the speaker’s resentment into an absurd, almost nightmarish vision. Together, these elements portray a figure who resists social expectations, practical purpose, and moral scrutiny, choosing instead passivity, aesthetic detachment, and imaginative defiance.
outputs.L4:
The speaker presents apathy not as simple indifference but as a deliberate form of self-protection. Throughout the work, surreal images of fishing gear, a witness stand, and pastoral idleness transform an internal conflict into a strange symbolic landscape. Each image suggests a different kind of pressure: the possibility of being caught, the demand to testify, and the temptation to escape responsibility by remaining inactive. Together, they reveal a speaker who wants to withdraw from the world while still feeling threatened by its expectations.

The imagery of fishing gear evokes entanglement, capture, and exposure. Hooks, lines, or nets imply that involvement with other people carries the risk of being seized and pulled into obligations the speaker would rather avoid. Writing creates a similar danger. To write is to make something private visible, to give others material they can interpret and judge. The pain of writing therefore comes not only from the effort of expression but also from the vulnerability it produces. Once thoughts have been put into words, the speaker can no longer remain entirely hidden or undefined.

This anxiety becomes sharper through the image of the witness stand. A witness is expected to remember accurately, speak clearly, and accept responsibility for a public account of events. Yet the speaker’s memory is unstable. Recollection appears fragmented, selective, or possibly distorted, making testimony both difficult and suspect. The courtroom-like setting turns social judgment into an almost legal ordeal: the speaker is not merely being observed but examined, challenged, and required to explain the self. Unreliable memory offers a possible escape from this demand, but it also prevents the speaker from establishing a secure personal history.

Against these threatening images, pastoral idleness seems to promise peace. The speaker imagines a state of passivity in which nothing must be produced, defended, or confessed. This retreat, however, is not wholly innocent. Idleness becomes a strategy for refusing accountability, while contempt allows the speaker to dismiss those who demand action. By treating others as foolish, coercive, or excessively determined, the speaker can present withdrawal as superiority rather than fear.

The willfulness of the speaker’s peers intensifies this conflict. They appear able—or at least willing—to choose, act, create, and judge. Their decisiveness makes the speaker’s passivity more visible. At the same time, the speaker resents them for imposing standards of purpose and consistency that feel invasive. Contempt thus functions as a defensive barrier: if the claims of others can be devalued, then the speaker need not answer them.

Ultimately, the surreal imagery portrays a self caught between exposure and disappearance. Fishing gear threatens capture, the witness stand demands a coherent testimony, and the pastoral scene offers the fantasy of indefinite retreat. Yet none of these positions provides genuine freedom. The speaker’s refusal to act preserves a degree of mystery, but it also produces isolation and paralysis. Apathy becomes both shelter and prison, leaving the self trapped between the demands of a willful social world and the desire to remain passive, unaccountable, and unknowable.
outputs.L5:
Dana, Ward, and Sarah had been friends for as long as they could remember. Dana was adventurous, Ward was thoughtful, and Sarah always knew how to bring people together.

One Saturday morning, they decided to explore an old trail outside their town. Along the way, Dana led them through the woods, Ward studied the map, and Sarah kept everyone laughing when the path became difficult. At the end of the trail, they discovered a quiet lake surrounded by wildflowers.

Sitting beside the water, the three friends realized that the journey had been memorable not because of the destination, but because they had experienced it together. Dana, Ward, and Sarah returned home tired but happy, already planning their next adventure.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental prose poem in the style of Dana Ward, using fishing gear, a drunken-night interrogation, shepherds, and the phrase “jealous cellmate.”
counterfactuals.output:
I can’t write in Dana Ward’s exact style, but I can offer an original experimental prose poem with fragmented, conversational lyricism, associative leaps, and surreal intimacy.

—

The tackle box opened like a bad alibi. Hooks in their little silver sleep, the bobbers red-eyed, the reel holding its black river of memory. At 2:17 a.m. you asked me where I’d been, then asked the lamp, then the wet sleeve of my coat. Each answer smelled of gin and pondweed. I said the shepherds had detained me at the edge of town, their flock spilling over the road like weather with teeth. You said shepherds don’t work nights. I said neither do I, apparently.

On the table, a lure glittered with the cheap authority of evidence. Exhibit A: feather. Exhibit B: bloodless barb. Exhibit C: my phone vibrating under an empty glass, my jealous cellmate, furious at every freedom I mistook for solitude.

You leaned closer. Who was she? The room tipped its bottle toward us. Outside, the shepherds counted backward, losing one sheep per number. I tried to explain that desire is only fishing gear abandoned in tall grass: line snarled around the moon, hook dressed as hunger, hands insisting the dark must contain something because the dark keeps moving.

You wrote this down on a napkin, misspelling hunger.

By dawn the interrogation had become a kind of prayer. Your questions softened, grew wool. The shepherds entered without knocking and filled the kitchen with bells. One placed a lamb in my lap; another confiscated the corkscrew. Nobody confessed. In the sink, minnows flashed among the glasses, brief coins in a ruined fountain.

Tell me again, you said.

So I told you: I cast my voice into the night and waited. What came back was not love, exactly, but the line tightening—proof that somewhere beyond sight, something had mistaken my wound for food.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a surreal, stream-of-consciousness paragraph about a lethargic speaker who compares ordinary objects to jewelry and refuses to explain what happened the night before.
counterfactuals.output: I am too tired to lift the morning off my chest, so I let it sit there, gray and purring, while the spoon in the sink shines like a bent silver brooch and three shirt buttons glitter on the floor like pearls escaped from a nervous queen. Don’t ask me about last night. The kettle wears steam like a diamond veil, the doorknob is a dull gold ring the house has forgotten to remove, and even the cracked bar of soap seems set with moonstones if I close one eye, which is all I have the strength to do. No, I won’t tell you why the hallway smells of rain or why my left shoe is full of sugar; explanations are such heavy furniture, and I can barely drag my thoughts from one side of the room to the other. Let yesterday keep its black necklace of hours—I am lying here beneath the jeweled ticking of the clock, waiting for noon to forget my name.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a dense contemporary poem dedicated to Dana Ward. Blend self-deprecation, direct address to “Sarah” and the reader, courtroom imagery, fishing, hell, and sleeping at the base of a hill.
counterfactuals.output:
**For Dana Ward, Below the Switchback**

Sarah, I have entered my plea:  
guilty of mistaking the hook for hunger,  
the river for a long blue sentence  
the judge might commute if I looked  
sufficiently ruined. I did. I always do.  
My face is cheap evidence.

Your Honor, the fish was already silver  
before I lied about catching it.  
Hell keeps such records—each barb,  
each mouth made briefly into a door.  
Sarah, don’t laugh: even the devil  
throws back what cannot praise him.

Reader, approach the bench.  
You have been selected from the dark  
to witness me sleeping at the base of a hill,  
my coat rolled beneath my skull,  
all ascent postponed until morning  
or the next century’s alarm.

Above me, houses burn their little squares  
of domestic gold. Below, worms revise  
the earth without applause. I dream  
the jury is twelve wet stones  
and every stone has Sarah’s voice:  
*Explain why you wanted to be forgiven  
before you had done anything worth forgiving.*

I cast into the night. The line  
comes back wearing nothing.  
This is my talent: extracting absence  
from abundance, calling it supper,  
then asking you, reader, to split the bill.

Dana, somewhere language is climbing  
without us, barefoot, carrying its own hell  
like a lantern. Sarah, let it go.  
The court is adjourned inside my chest.  
The fish flash once in the black water,  
innocent as knives.

I remain downhill, asleep—  
a poor exhibit, a collapsed argument—  
while dawn, that ruthless bailiff,  
calls every living thing to rise.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an avant-garde monologue with minimal conventional structure, ampersands, abrupt associative shifts, and a tone that moves between comic cuteness, contempt, exhaustion, and metaphysical despair.
counterfactuals.output:
& the moon arrives in a tiny hat

as if this helps

as if the oceans have not been dragging their blue furniture from room to room all night

“Oh,” says the moon, “I’m management.”

adorable  
vile little lantern  
pimple of eternity

I file a complaint with the nearest moth. The moth eats the complaint & then my sleeve & then, ceremonially, the concept of Tuesday.

good for her

somewhere a machine is learning to apologize without feeling tired. I, meanwhile, am feeling tired with astonishing precision. My exhaustion has little silver instruments. It measures the distance between the bed & the obligation. It says: impossible. It says: crawl, citizen. It says: have you tried turning your soul off & on again?

& there is a rabbit in the supermarket

no, not literally

worse

a rabbit in the architecture  
a softness trapped in the fluorescent instructions  
BUY TWO  
SAVE NOTHING  
DIE WITH POINTS

I put a strawberry in my basket because it resembles a heart that has successfully unionized.

ha ha

the cashier asks if I found everything.

Everything?

I found toothpaste. I found twelve brands of water pretending to have personalities. I found the old abyss behind the yogurt, shivering in a promotional vest.

I did not report it.

snitches get cosmologies

& suddenly childhood, sticky as a boiled sweet: a plastic dinosaur on the radiator, its green body bending toward extinction. I loved it. Of course I loved it. Love is what we call our panic when it fits in the palm.

tiny roar  
tiny teeth  
tiny doomed king

then the pivot, the invoice, the bloodwork, the password containing one uppercase letter & one symbol of genuine remorse

I choose:

GODisAway_7

weak password, says the screen

yes

yes, I know

Outside, people carry coffees like votive candles. Their faces say: commute. Their shoes say: we have forgiven gravity for now. A pigeon struts through the crosswalk with the confidence of a minor despot.

I respect him  
I despise him  
I would vote for him

what platform?

crumbs & vengeance

At noon, my body becomes a committee. The knees oppose. The stomach abstains. The brain proposes another memory of embarrassment from fifteen years ago. Motion carried unanimously.

& somewhere, beneath language, a little pink animal is sleeping

perhaps hope

perhaps an organ no longer covered by insurance

don’t wake it

Let it dream that existence is not the universe’s longest administrative error. Let it dream of peaches, warm laundry, a hand resting briefly on another hand without ownership, without prophecy, without the terrible customer survey afterward.

Would you recommend being alive to a friend?

0 1 2 3 4 5

I press all the buttons.

The machine begins to smoke.

At last, a result.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a single-paragraph prose poem beginning with “with Dana Ward,” featuring the repeated opening phrase, the line “On the witness stand I am a kitten,” and ending with the speaker murmuring “jealous cellmate” as peers pass by.
counterfactuals.output: with Dana Ward, I inventory the blue hours by touch; with Dana Ward, I teach every locked door to dream of hinges, while rain rehearses its soft testimony against the windows. On the witness stand I am a kitten, paws folded over the record, my small heart purring beneath the prosecutor’s thunder. With Dana Ward, I remember that tenderness is contraband only until someone shares it, that every sentence has a hidden courtyard where language paces beneath the moon. The bell rings, the corridor opens, and as my peers pass by, bright with their temporary freedom, I lower my eyes and murmur “jealous cellmate”
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
